title: Burst fallback orchestrator and fidelity lanes PRD (rough)
body:
Purpose:
This doc describes a proposed operator, the Burst Fallback Orchestrator (BFO), and a related concept we call fidelity lanes. The goal is to let Dedicated customers safely accept bursty traffic while preserving tenant isolation and latency SLOs via automated graceful degradation and clear runbooks. This is a working PRD — experimental design and simulation-first approach.

Problem statement:
- Tenants on Dedicated pools produce unpredictable microbursts and seasonal spikes. Current autoscalers either overprovision (costly) or throttle abruptly (bad UX).
- During capacity contention, we need deterministic, observable fallbacks rather than opaque throttles.
- Isolation: noisy tenants can degrade other tenants’ p99 latency; hard preemption causes SLO violations and support churn.

High-level proposal:
1) Burst Fallback Orchestrator (BFO): a control-plane service that consumes rich telemetry (queue depth, runtime concurrency, per-tenant tail latency, token burn rates) and outputs deterministic fallback decisions. The BFO is policy-driven and pluggable (rules + ML heuristic).
2) Fidelity lanes: categorize request handling into lanes by fidelity/quality (e.g., full-fidelity, fast-summary, token-reduced, best-effort). When contention is detected, requests are steered to lower-fidelity lanes based on tenant policy, request class, and SLO budgets.
3) Tenant-level soft currency: each tenant has a burst credit balance (earned via commit/consume model). Credits are debited on high-cost requests; when depleted, tenant moves to degraded lane rather than being hard-evicted.

Key goals and success metrics:
- Reduce hard preemptions by 70% in simulated overloads.
- Keep p99 latency for high-fidelity lanes within committed SLOs for paying tiers 95% of the time.
- Show measurable cost savings vs simply doubling reserved capacity (target 20–35% savings for common burst profile).
- Clear observability: per-tenant fallback rate, lane distribution, average quality delta.

Policy primitives (what operators can configure) :
- Fidelity ladder (names, degradation semantics, e.g., truncate tokens, disable long-form completion, use quantized model variant).
- Credit accrual and decay (how many burst tokens per hour/day per commitment).
- Priority rules (tier > scheduled job > internal infra).
- Safety fences: absolute hard-throttle thresholds for cluster-stability emergencies.

Behavioral flow (simplified):
- Normal: requests routed to requested model variant and full-fidelity lane. Credits untouched.
- Pre-surge detection: BFO detects velocity/telemetry pattern (queue slope + GPU overload signal) -> mark pool "hot" and start prewarm suggestions.
- Burst active: BFO evaluates tenants by policy + credit. If contention persists:
  * Best-effort step-down: move new requests to the next lower fidelity lane.
  * Preserve in-flight high-fidelity requests to completion when possible.
  * If cluster health degrades, escalate to circuit-breaker hard-throttle for low-priority tenants.

Implementation notes and system interactions:
- Data plane vs control plane: BFO runs in control plane; it emits lightweight routing directives to the traffic router and to per-worker admission controllers.
- Telemetry feed: requires enriched metrics (per-tenant tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99, kv-cache hit rates, batch sizes). We will leverage existing Console traces and add a compact streaming telemetry contract.
- Model variants: fidelity lanes should map to explicit model variants when available (e.g., quantized small, truncated prompt flow) or to runtime knobs (max tokens, stop sequences, sampling temperature).
- Backwards compatibility: default policy when not configured is conservative: allow short bursts, prefer quick degradation to hard eviction.

Operational playbooks / runbooks:
- On high-burn event: BFO sets tenants into degraded lanes, ops page is created with affected tenants list and the dominant failure signal.
- Customer notifications: automated email or webhook with reason (e.g., "your traffic exceeded burst credits and was routed to reduced-fidelity lane") and remediation steps (increase commitment, optimize prompts, enable burst purchase).
- Rollback: feature flag to disable BFO per-pool and per-tenant; can revert to existing autoscaler in emergency.

Monitoring and telemetry (concrete metrics):
- Per-tenant: fallback-rate (ratio of requests served in degraded lanes), average fidelity-score (0..1), credit-balance, p95/p99 latency.
- Pool-level: lane-distribution histogram, hard-throttle-count, queue-slope.
- Alerts: rising fallback-rate > 10% for 10m for premium tenant; pool hard-throttle > 0.5% -> pager.

Simulations and experiments:
- Build a simulator that replays production traces (we have anonymized traces) to test policy combos: credit sizing, grace windows, lane thresholds.
- Initial offline experiments target 1000-tenant replay with burst profiles (flash-sale, nightly-batch collision).

Privacy and security considerations:
- Per-tenant telemetry is sensitive; ensure only necessary aggregates are emitted to the BFO and retained per policy.
- For Private deployments, BFO runs in customer-managed control plane; credentials and KMS access follow private deployment patterns.

Open design questions (prioritized):
1) How to define fidelity semantics for arbitrary customer prompts without breaking correctness? (Need safe defaults + customer opt-in for aggressive degradations.)
2) Credit economics: free accrual vs paid burst purchases — what price elasticity do we expect? (GTM input needed.)
3) How to simulate worst-case cascade when multiple tenants degrade simultaneously? (We need a chaos test harness.)

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (2 weeks): Spec + telemetry contract + simulation harness.
- Phase 1 (6 weeks): Implement BFO prototype + one fidelity lane (token-truncate) + router hook. Internal-only testing with synthetic traffic.
- Phase 2 (8 weeks): Canary with 5 low-risk tenants on Dedicated pools (feature flag). Observe fallback rates and customer UX.
- Phase 3 (ongoing): Expand lanes, add ML-based scoring, integrate Console alerts and billing signals.

Risks and mitigations:
- Customer surprise: degrade quality without explicit consent -> mitigation: default to opt-in for aggressive fidelity and provide transparent notifications + trial credits.
- Complexity of policy surface -> mitigation: provide sane presets (conservative, balanced, aggressive) and UI helpers in Console.
- Telemetry lag -> mitigation: prefer fast, lossy signals for BFO decisions and require a final control check at admission.

Appendix: small examples
- Example policy: "premium-slo": keep premium tenants in full-fidelity until credit balance < 20%, then route new requests to token-reduced lane; never hard-throttle unless cluster health critical.
- Example lane mapping: full-fidelity -> model-x/32k, token-reduced -> model-x/8k + stop early at 512 tokens, summary-lane -> model-small/2k + aggressive top-p.

Next steps / immediate action items:
- Product: finalize lane primitives and customer presets.
- Applied ML: design scoring baseline for criticality of requests.
- Infra/Serving: prototype lightweight routing directives and per-worker admission hook.
- Solutions Eng / CS: pick 3 pilot customers for Phase 2.

Notes to self: keep the PRD lean; this is intentionally mechanic-first so we can iterate on the simulator. Avoid hard promises on cost savings until we have replay numbers.
